title: The Nuniyya of Ibn Zaydun
intro: Al-Maqqari calls it “the Nuniyya of Ibn Zaydun”, and the sources tell its occasion in different ways. Al-Fath ibn Khaqan says that Ibn Zaydun, kept from Wallada after he had turned the Banu Jahwar against him, wrote it to her when he despaired of seeing her again, to hold her to her pledge and excuse his absence by the ordeal that had overtaken him; al-Marrakushi says he composed it in Seville, longing for “the daughter of al-Mahdi” in Cordoba; Ibn Bassam quotes it among his love poems without naming anyone, beginning at “You went away and so did we” (line 12 here). It mourns the parting and the enemies' delight, recalls the days of union, sends greetings by lightning and the east wind, describes the beloved as a child of kings made of musk, calls her garden, life and paradise, and ends with a plea for faithfulness and a farewell. Al-Safadi says it grew so famous that people said whoever learnt it by heart would die far from home, and poets imitated it, from Abu Bakr ibn al-Milh, as Ibn Bassam records, to Ahmad Shawqi in modern times.

translation: Now being apart has replaced our being close,
and coldness between us has taken the place of sweet meetings.
1.sharh: Distance has taken the place of closeness, and estrangement has replaced the joy of meeting. The opening line rhymes in both halves and sets each word against its opposite: apart against together, coldness against the sweetness of meeting.

translation: If only, as the morning of parting dawned, death had come for us,
and our herald had risen to announce our end.
2.sharh: He wishes death had taken him on the morning of the parting, so that a herald would have announced his death before he had to live through it. The editors Kamil Kilani and Abd al-Rahman Khalifa explain that death parts lovers by force, while estrangement parts them by choice, and so is worse.

translation: Who will tell those whose going has clothed us
in a grief that time cannot wear out, though it wears us out,
3.sharh: He asks who will carry a message to the loved ones whose departure has dressed him in a grief that time never wears thin, though it wears him thin. The question runs on into the next line, which gives the message.

translation: that the time which always made us laugh,
glad of their nearness, has turned to making us weep.
4.sharh: This is the message: the time that used to make them laugh, happy in their loved ones' company, now makes them weep. Laughter and tears stand at either end of the line, to show how completely time has turned.

translation: Our enemies, enraged that we poured love for each other, prayed
that we would choke on it, and Time said “Amen”.
5.sharh: Their enemies, enraged to see the lovers pour love for each other like wine, prayed that they would choke on it, and Time said “Amen”. The whole image is drawn from drinking: love is the cup, and parting is the drink that sticks in the throat.

translation: What had been knotted in our souls came undone,
and what had joined our hands was cut.
6.sharh: What was knotted between their souls came undone, and what joined their hands was cut. The pledge of the heart and the touch of the hand were both lost: nothing binds them now, inwardly or outwardly.

translation: Once we were such that no one feared our parting;
today we are such that no one hopes for our meeting.
7.sharh: Once they were together and there was no fear of parting; now they are apart and there is no hope of meeting. Each word of the first half meets its opposite in the second: then and now, fear and hope, parting and meeting.

translation: I wish I knew, when we have never pleased your enemies,
whether our enemies have won any favour from you.
8.sharh: He wonders whether his enemies have won the beloved's favour, when he has never sought to please the beloved's enemies. He has stayed loyal, and fears that the other side has made peace with those who wish him harm.

translation: Since you left we have held no conviction but loyalty to you,
nor taken up any other faith.
9.sharh: Since they left he has held no belief but faithfulness to them, and taken up no other faith. He speaks of loyalty in the language of religion: a conviction one holds and a creed one wears.

translation: It is not our due that you gladden an envier's eye
with us, or delight those who hate us.
10.sharh: He deserves better than to have them delight the envious and gladden those who secretly hate him. Their coldness, he implies, serves no one but his enemies.

translation: We used to think despair, when it came, would console us;
now we despair, and why does despair only spur us on?
11.sharh: He used to believe that despair, once it came, would console him; now that he truly despairs, despair only drives his love on. The editors Kilani and Khalifa compare Majnun's reproach to his own heart, which promised to give Layla up and did not.

translation: You went away, and so did we; our breasts have not cooled
with longing for you, nor have our eyes run dry.
12.sharh: They went far away and so did he, yet his breast has not cooled from longing, nor have his eyes dried. Wet and dry trade places: the ribs stay parched with longing, the eyes stay wet. Ibn Bassam and al-Fath ibn Khaqan both begin the poem here.

translation: When our hearts whisper to you, grief almost
puts an end to us, but for the comfort we give ourselves.
13.sharh: Whenever his heart speaks to them in secret across the distance, grief all but kills him; only the comfort he gives himself keeps him alive. The heart talks to the absent beloved as if they were close.

translation: Our days have changed with losing you and turned
black, while with you our nights were white.
14.sharh: Since he lost them his days have turned black, while with them his nights were white. He inverts the natural order: light and dark now follow the beloved's presence, not the sun.

translation: when the face of life was bright with our closeness,
and the haunt of pleasure clear, as we were clear with each other,
15.sharh: He remembers when life was bright because they were in harmony, and their place of pleasure was clear as their affection was pure. Most of the old sources read “the watering place of pleasure”, which makes the clearness that of water.

translation: and when we bent down the boughs of union, their fruit
hanging low, and picked from them whatever we wished.
16.sharh: Union was like a fruit tree: they bent its boughs down, the fruit hanging within reach, and picked whatever they wished. Kilani and Khalifa explain funun here as boughs, the plural of fanan.

translation: May rain water your days, the days of joy, for you
were nothing to our souls but fragrant herbs.
17.sharh: He prays for rain on the time they shared, the time of joy, for they were sweet herbs to his soul. Praying for rain on a place or a time is the old Arabic blessing; here the blessing falls on happy days.

translation: Do not think your being far from us has changed us
because distance has so often changed those who love.
18.sharh: He tells them not to assume that distance has changed him just because distance so often changes lovers. He knows what separation does to others and insists he is the exception.

translation: By God, our desires have sought no substitute
for you, nor have our hopes turned away from you.
19.sharh: He swears that his desires have looked for no one in their place and his hopes have turned to no one else. Another reading, which Kilani and Khalifa record, has “taken up nothing new”: no fresh love has replaced the old.

translation: Night-travelling lightning, go to the palace at dawn and rain
on the one who used to pour us love and affection undiluted.
20.sharh: He calls on the lightning travelling by night to reach the palace at dawn and pour its rain on the one who used to give him pure love to drink. Rain is the blessing returned for love given.

translation: And ask there whether thinking of us troubles
a dear one whom thinking of has come to trouble us.
21.sharh: He asks the lightning to find out whether remembering him torments the beloved as the beloved's memory torments him. He wants to know if the pain of remembrance is shared.

translation: And east wind, carry our greeting
to one whose greeting, even from afar, would bring us to life.
22.sharh: He sends his greeting with the east wind to one whose greeting, even from far away, would bring him back to life. Arabic plays on hayya, “greeted”, and yuhyi, “gives life”: a greeting from her is life itself.

translation: Will I see Time repay us with some kindness
of its own, when we never pressed it only now and then?
23.sharh: He wonders whether Time will ever pay what it owes him by granting a meeting, since he has pressed Time for it constantly, not just now and then. Meeting is a debt and he the creditor, dunning Time without pause.

translation: Reared in royalty, as if God had made him
of musk, and ordained that all others be made of clay,
24.sharh: The beloved was raised in a royal house, and seems to have been made of musk, while God ordained that everyone else be made of clay. The sources that name the addressee make her Wallada, daughter of al-Mustakfi; the poem speaks of the beloved here in the masculine.

translation: or cast him from pure silver and crowned him
with bright gold, to make a marvel and a beauty.
25.sharh: Or as if God had cast him in pure silver and crowned him with bright gold, as a work of art. Ali Abd al-Azim reads the silver as a fair face and the golden crown as fair hair.

translation: When he sways, his strings of pearls are a burden to his delicacy,
and his anklets draw blood from his softness.
26.sharh: When he sways as he walks, the pearls of his necklaces weigh him down and his anklets make his skin bleed, so delicate is he. Luxury has made the beloved too tender to bear jewellery.

translation: The sun was his wet-nurse in his curtained bed,
or rather, he showed himself to her only now and then.
27.sharh: The sun was his nurse only inside his curtained bed; no, he showed himself to the sun only now and then. He was kept so sheltered that the sun hardly saw him, which completes the picture of a pampered child of kings.

translation: As if the bright stars had been set
in the plane of his cheek, as amulet and adornment.
28.sharh: It is as if the bright stars had been set in the plane of his cheek, both to adorn him and, like amulets, to guard him from envious eyes, as Kilani and Khalifa explain.

translation: What harm is it that we were not his equal in rank?
In love, our matching each other is enough.
29.sharh: It does no harm that he is not the beloved's equal in rank; in love, being equal in love is enough. Kafin, “enough”, chimes with takafina, “our matching each other”: love makes equals of unequals.

translation: Garden, where our glances have so often gathered
roses that the east wind brought out fresh, and eglantine;
30.sharh: He calls the beloved a garden where his eyes have long gathered fresh roses, brought out by the east wind, and white eglantine. His eyes pick them only by looking. The editors leave the image unexplained; the likelier reading is that the roses and eglantine are the red and white of her cheeks.

translation: Life, whose bloom let us enjoy at length
hopes of every kind and pleasures of every sort;
31.sharh: She is life itself, whose bloom he enjoyed at length, tasting hopes of every kind and pleasures of many sorts. Her days with him were the flower of his life.

translation: Bliss, in whose plenty we strutted, and for a while
trailed the hem of a robe embroidered with good fortune.
32.sharh: She is the bliss in whose plenty he once strutted, trailing the hem of a figured robe of good fortune. Good fortune is a garment, ample and patterned, that he once wore and has now lost.

translation: We do not say your name, out of reverence and respect;
your high station spares us that.
33.sharh: He does not speak her name, out of reverence; her high standing makes naming her unnecessary. Ali Abd al-Azim explains this line and the next together: he guards her name out of reverence, and she is so singular that the least hint is enough.

translation: Since you stand alone, sharing no quality with anyone,
the description is enough to make it plain and clear.
34.sharh: Since no one shares any of her qualities, describing her is enough to identify her. Anyone who hears the description knows whom it means. Ali Abd al-Azim notes that Baha' al-Din Zuhayr later took up the idea.

translation: Garden of eternity, for your lote tree
and sweet Kawthar we have been given zaqqum and ghislin.
35.sharh: She was his paradise, and he has been given, in exchange for its lote tree and its sweet river of Kawthar, the bitter tree of hell and the festering drink of the damned. Losing her is a fall from heaven into hell, in the Quran's own words.

translation: If meeting has grown too rare in this world, then
we will meet you at the stations of the Gathering, and that suffices.
36.sharh: If meeting has become impossible in this life, he will meet her on the Day of Judgement, and that is enough for him. Hope moves to the next world. The line is not in the manuscripts of the Diwan; Ali Abd al-Azim added it from al-Fath ibn Khaqan, and al-Marrakushi also has it.

translation: As if we had not spent the night with union as our third,
and good fortune lowering our tell-tale's eyelids.
37.sharh: Now it is as if he had never spent those nights with her, with union as the only third between them, while good fortune closed the slanderer's eyes. Kilani and Khalifa explain that luck put the informer to sleep, so he told no tales.

translation: Two secrets in the mind of the dark, which kept us hidden
until the tongue of morning almost gave us away.
38.sharh: The two lovers were secrets kept in the mind of the night, until the tongue of dawn nearly gave them away. Ibn Bassam judged that the charm of this metaphor improves on al-Mutanabbi's line about the dark that shields a lover and the dawn that betrays him.

translation: No wonder we spoke of grief, though reason
forbade it, and left patience forgotten.
39.sharh: It is no wonder that he spoke of his grief though reason forbade it, and left patience forgotten. Nahat, “forbade”, plays on nuha, “reason”, so called because it forbids; even reason could not restrain him.

translation: On the day of parting we read grief like suras
written down, and learnt patience only by rote.
40.sharh: On the day of parting he read grief like written chapters of scripture, while patience he took only by rote. The editors do not explain it; the likelier sense is that grief is a text he knows by heart, while patience is something he repeats but does not own.

translation: As for your love, we never ranked any other drink
with its spring, though it quenches us only to make us thirst.
41.sharh: He has never put any other love on a level with hers, though the more he drinks of it the thirstier he grows. Ibn Bassam calls the thirst that drinking only increases a well-worn idea, best known from Ibn al-Rumi's lines on a lover's kiss.

translation: We did not shun a sky of beauty whose star you are
because we had got over it, nor leave it out of hate.
42.sharh: He did not turn from the sky of beauty whose star she is because he had forgotten her, nor leave it out of hatred. The reason, as the next line says, was force.

translation: Nor did we avoid it by choice when it was near;
it was against our will that obstacles kept us away.
43.sharh: Nor did he keep away from that sky by choice, while it was near; obstacles drove him away against his will. Ali Abd al-Azim explains that he was forced to leave her though her house was close.

translation: We grieve for you when the mixed wine is passed
quickly round among us, and our singers sing.
44.sharh: He grieves for her when diluted wine is passed briskly round and the singers sing. Kilani and Khalifa explain that he misses her company at the gathering: the pleasures that make others forget only remind him she is gone.

translation: The cups of wine bring out in our nature
no sign of cheer, and the strings do not distract us.
45.sharh: Wine brings no sign of cheer to his face, and the lute strings cannot distract him. Neither wine nor music has any hold on him now.

translation: Stay true to our pledge as long as we do;
the free repay in fairness what they are paid.
46.sharh: He asks her to keep faith for as long as he does, since a free and noble person repays fairly what he is given. The second half echoes the proverb kama tadinu tudan, “as you treat others, so you will be treated”.

translation: We have taken no companion in your place to keep us,
nor gained any other love to turn us from you.
47.sharh: He has taken no other companion in her place who might hold him, nor gained any other beloved who might turn him from her. His heart has found neither a substitute nor a way out.

translation: Even if the full moon of the dark leaned towards us
from its high rising, it would not, saving you, win our love.
48.sharh: Even if the full moon leaned down to him from its high rising place, it would not win his heart, and he begs her pardon for even comparing her with it. The moon, to which beauties are compared, is no rival.

translation: Grant us faithfulness, though you grant no meeting;
your phantom will content us, and remembering will be enough.
49.sharh: He asks her to give him faithfulness even if she gives him no meeting; her image in his dreams will content him, and remembering her will suffice. He has come down to asking for very little.

translation: And a reply would be a joy, if you added to it
the white hands of favour you have always held out to us.
50.sharh: A reply from her would be a joy, if she added to it the generous kindness she has always shown. Ali Abd al-Azim reads the close of the poem as the hope of a letter from her.

translation: Upon you from us be God's peace as long as there remains
a love for you that we hide, and that hides us.
51.sharh: He ends by sending God's peace for as long as his love remains, a love he hides and that hides him. Kilani and Khalifa read the last word as takhfina, “reveals us”, an old sense of the verb: the passion he hides gives him away. Abd al-Azim prints tukhfina, “hides us”, without comment.

1.2.4.head: لُقيان
1.2.4.meaning: Our meeting. Al-Maqqari's Nafh al-Tib has dunyana, “our world”.

2.1.1.meaning: Alla: “if only”, “why did it not”; a particle of regret.

2.1.4-5.meaning: “The morning of parting”: the dawn of the day they separated.

2.2.5.head: النّاعي
2.2.5.meaning: Our herald of death, who brings the news. Ali Abd al-Azim's edition has da'ina, “our caller”.

3.1.3.head: المُلبِس
3.1.3.meaning: Those who clothed us: grief is a garment they put on him.

5.2.2.head: غَصَّ
5.2.2.meaning: Choke: when a drink sticks in the throat.

7.1.1-2.meaning: “And we would be”: once we were. Al-Maqqari has “Yesterday we were”.

8.1.1-3.meaning: “Would that I knew”: shi'r here is knowing, not poetry.

8.2.5.meaning: Utba: favour restored after reproach, reconciliation.

9.2.3.head: تَقَلَّدَ
9.2.3.meaning: Take up, as one wears a sword or a necklace; here, adopt a faith.

10.2.5.head: الكاشِح
10.2.5.meaning: Kashih: an enemy who hides his hatred.

12.1.5.head: الجَوانِح
12.1.5.meaning: Jawanih: the ribs over the heart; the breast.

12.2.5.head: المَآقي
12.2.5.meaning: Ma'aqi: the inner corners of the eyes, where tears run.

15.2.1.head: المَربَع
15.2.1.meaning: Marba': a spring encampment, a place to stay.

16.1.2.head: هَصَرَ
16.1.2.meaning: Bent down a bough to pick from it.

17.1.1.head: سَقى
17.1.1.meaning: “May it be watered”: a prayer for rain on a place or a time, an old Arabic blessing.

17.2.4.head: الرَّياحين
17.2.4.meaning: Rayahin: fragrant plants, sweet herbs such as basil.

18.2.1.meaning: “Because”. So the reciter and Ibn Bassam; both editions of the Diwan print in, “indeed”.

20.1.2-3.meaning: “Night-traveller of the lightning”: lightning moving across the night sky, which promised rain.

20.2.3.head: الصِّرف
20.2.3.meaning: Sirf: unmixed, neat, said of wine; here, pure love.

21.2.1.head: الإِلف
21.2.1.meaning: Ilf: an intimate, the one you are used to; the beloved.

22.1.3.meaning: Saba: the east wind, which blows from where the sun rises.

23.2.5.head: الغِبّ
23.2.5.meaning: Ghibb: every other day, now and then; here, seldom.

24.1.1-2.meaning: “Nursling of kingship”: raised in a royal house.

27.1.6.head: الأَكِلَّة
27.1.6.meaning: Kilal: fine curtains hung like a tent against mosquitoes.

28.2.3.head: التَّعويذ
28.2.3.meaning: Ta'widh: an amulet against the evil eye.

30.2.5.head: النِّسرين
30.2.5.meaning: Nisrin: a fragrant white rose, eglantine.

35.1.5.head: السِّدرَة
35.1.5.meaning: Sidra: the lote tree, which the Quran places in paradise. Most old sources read salsal, “its sweet water”.

35.2.1.head: الكَوثَر
35.2.1.meaning: Kawthar: a river of paradise named in the Quran (108:1).

35.2.3.head: الزَّقّوم
35.2.3.meaning: Zaqqum: the tree of hell whose fruit the damned eat (Quran 44:43–44).

35.2.4.head: الغِسلين
35.2.4.meaning: Ghislin: the filth that flows from the damned, their food in the Quran (69:36).

36.2.1-2.meaning: “The stations of the Gathering”: the Day of Judgement, when all are gathered and stand to be judged.

37.2.6.head: الواشي
37.2.6.meaning: Washi: the informer, the slanderer who carries tales between lovers.

40.2.4.head: التَّلقين
40.2.4.meaning: Talqin: learning by being prompted, by rote.

44.1.5.head: المُشَعشَع
44.1.5.meaning: Mixed with water, as wine was drunk.

48.2.5.head: حاشا
48.2.5.meaning: “Saving you”: with all respect to you, who are beyond comparison.

49.2.1.head: الطَّيف
49.2.1.meaning: Tayf: the beloved's phantom, seen in dreams.

50.2.1-2.meaning: “White hands”: generous favours; hand in Arabic also means a kindness done.

51.2.4.head: أَخفى
51.2.4.meaning: Hides us; the verb khafa, without the prefix, means both “hid” and “showed”.
